title: Many causes of death
hook: alarms treat waking up as the default; Nagarjuna calls it a wonder, because life is a bubble in the wind
tomorrow: can the very things that keep you alive also hurt you?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the weaver's daughter: I know I will die; I don't know when. The time is uncertain. No one knows when. Today, why.

Nobody's alarm says congratulations. It just rings, as if waking up were guaranteed and only the time was in question. Here's a strange line, from a letter of advice written by the Buddhist philosopher Nagarjuna to a king. It's a wonder, he writes, that after breathing out a person breathes in again, and that after sleeping a person wakes up. A wonder? Breathing in? Waking up? The most ordinary things there are. That's today's puzzle.
screen: `NO ALARM SAYS CONGRATULATIONS.` → `BREATHING IN AGAIN: A WONDER?` → `TODAY'S PUZZLE.`

segments.voice: Nagarjuna was an Indian philosopher of the Mahayana, and his Letter to a Friend is practical advice for a busy ruler. Just before the wonder, he gives the reason. Life, he says, runs on among many dangers, more fragile than a bubble in the wind. That's the key. If a life were sturdy, waking up would be nothing special. But if it's a bubble in the wind, every morning it's still there is the surprise. The sutta for dusk, a few days back, named some of those dangers plainly: a snake, a stumble, a meal that turns. Teachers of Atisha's roots fold the same point into the second root: the causes of death are many, and the body is fragile. Here's what the puzzle does. Usually, staying alive is the background, and dying is the shocking event. Nagarjuna flips the picture. Dying is the background, the thing a bubble does sooner or later. Staying alive is the event. And once it's flipped, ordinary things light up. A breath coming in. A heartbeat nobody asked for. Opening your eyes to a ceiling you've seen over and over. None of it was owed. This isn't meant to make anyone anxious about every snack and staircase. It's meant to turn a plain morning into a gift that arrived again. Fragile, and here.
screen: `A LETTER TO A KING.` · `A BUBBLE IN THE WIND.` · `DYING IS THE BACKGROUND.` · `STAYING ALIVE IS THE EVENT.` · then, large: `FRAGILE.`

segments.voice: Count, slowly, three things your body did for you today without being asked: woke you, breathed all night, carried you somewhere. With each one, give it a quiet thank you. Then sit with whatever is still working right now, and let it be enough.
Many causes of death: the body is fragile, a bubble in the wind, so each morning it's still here is a wonder.
Hold this today: fragile, and here, and that's the wonder. See you tomorrow, if the bubble holds.

chat.says: ông now says every morning, 'woke up again, what a wonder.' dark joke or what?
options: Not a joke. Life's that fragile, so waking really is a wonder to him.
Dark joke. He's making fun of death so he won't feel scared.
A polite phrase. It doesn't really mean anything to him.
chat.meaning: Nagarjuna calls waking a wonder because life is more fragile than a bubble in the wind. Ông is treating each morning as a gift.

tie.story: Nagarjuna wrote to a king that it's a wonder to breathe in again and to wake after sleep.
